subject: science
name: Materials Around Us
summary: Objects around us are made of materials such as wood, metal, plastic, glass, paper and cloth. Materials have properties — appearance (lustrous or non-lustrous), hardness, solubility in water, whether they float or sink, and transparency — and we group materials by these properties and choose materials for objects based on them. Everything that has mass and takes up space is called matter.

topics.title: Objects and materials
topics.summary: An object is a thing with a shape and a use; a material is what it is made of. One object can be made of different materials, and one material can make many objects.
topics.simple: A chair, a spoon and a bottle are **objects**. What they are made of — wood, steel, plastic, glass — is called a **material**. A chair can be made of wood, plastic or metal, and wood can be used to make a chair, a door or a pencil.
topics.explain:
Look around your classroom: desks, chairs, books, windows, bags, water bottles. Each of these is an **object**. The stuff an object is made of is its **material**.

Common materials: wood, metal (iron, steel, aluminium, copper), plastic, glass, paper, cloth (cotton, wool), rubber, clay, stone, leather.

Two important ideas:
- **The same object can be made from different materials:** a glass (tumbler) can be of glass, steel, plastic or copper; a ball can be of rubber, leather, plastic or cloth
- **The same material can make different objects:** wood is used for doors, tables, pencils and cricket bats; plastic for buckets, bottles, toys and pens

Some objects use **more than one material**: a pencil has wood and graphite; a pressure cooker has a metal body, a rubber gasket and a plastic handle.

**Choosing materials:** we pick a material based on what the object must do. A cooking pan is made of metal because it can take heat; its handle is plastic or wood because these don't get hot quickly. Different sports use different balls: a hard leather ball for cricket, a light hollow plastic ball for table tennis, a rubber ball that bounces well for many games.
topics.example: A school bag may be made of cloth or nylon (strong and flexible), with metal or plastic zips, plastic buckles and foam padding — each material chosen for a job.
keyPoints: Object = a thing with a shape and use; material = what it's made of
One object can be made of different materials
One material can make many objects
Many objects use more than one material
Materials are chosen according to the object's use

topics.title: Appearance (lustre) and hardness
topics.summary: Lustrous materials, like most metals, are shiny; non-lustrous ones, like wood and paper, are dull. Hard materials are difficult to scratch or press; soft ones are easy to scratch or compress.
topics.simple: Some materials **shine**, like a new steel spoon, gold or copper — they are **lustrous**. Others look **dull**, like wood, paper and clay — they are **non-lustrous**. Some materials are **hard** (difficult to scratch or press, like iron and stone), while others are **soft** (easy to press or scratch, like cotton and sponge).
topics.explain:
**Appearance — lustre**
- **Lustrous** materials have a **shine** on their surface. Most **metals** are lustrous: gold, silver, copper, aluminium, steel.
- **Non-lustrous** materials look **dull**: wood, paper, cloth, clay, rubber.
- Metals can lose their shine when exposed to air and moisture for a long time (iron rusts, copper turns dull or greenish, silver turns black). If you rub or cut them, the fresh surface shines again.

**Hardness**
- **Hard** materials are **difficult to scratch or compress**: iron, steel, stone, glass, diamond.
- **Soft** materials are **easy to scratch or compress**: cotton, sponge, wax, chalk, rubber eraser.
- A simple test: try scratching the material with a steel key or a fingernail. If it gets scratched easily, it is soft.
- Hardness is a **comparison**: wood is harder than sponge but softer than iron.

**Using these properties**
- Jewellery and decorations use lustrous metals like gold and silver
- Tools, building materials and cooking pots use hard materials
- Pillows, mattresses and cushions use soft materials like cotton and foam
topics.example: An old copper vessel kept in the kitchen looks dull. When your grandmother scrubs it with lemon and salt, the shiny, lustrous surface appears again.
keyPoints: Lustrous = shiny (most metals: gold, copper, steel)
Non-lustrous = dull (wood, paper, clay)
Metals may go dull in air; a fresh cut surface shines
Hard = difficult to scratch or compress (iron, stone)
Soft = easy to scratch or compress (cotton, sponge, wax)
Hardness is relative — compare materials

topics.title: Soluble or insoluble, floating or sinking
topics.summary: Substances that dissolve in water, like salt and sugar, are soluble; those that don't, like sand and chalk, are insoluble. Some objects float on water (wood, cork, oil) and others sink (stone, iron nail).
topics.simple: Stir a spoon of **sugar** in water and it disappears — sugar is **soluble**. Stir **sand** in water and it stays at the bottom — sand is **insoluble**. Some things, like a cork or a dry leaf, **float** on water, while a stone or an iron nail **sinks**.
topics.explain:
**Solubility in water**
- A substance that **dissolves** completely and seems to disappear in water is **soluble**: salt, sugar, glucose, lemon juice
- A substance that **does not dissolve**, even after stirring well, is **insoluble**: sand, chalk powder, sawdust, wax, stones
- **ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution)** is made by dissolving salt and sugar in clean water; it is given to replace water and salts lost from the body during diarrhoea or dehydration

**Liquids in water**
- Some liquids **mix completely** with water: lemon juice, vinegar, milk
- Some **don't mix** and form a separate layer: coconut oil, mustard oil, kerosene

**Gases** can dissolve in water too. Fish and other water animals breathe the oxygen dissolved in water.

**Floating and sinking**
- Objects that stay on the surface **float**: wood, cork, dry leaves, a plastic ball, oil
- Objects that go down **sink**: stone, iron nail, coin, glass marble

These properties are useful: solubility helps us make sharbat, tea and ORS; insolubility helps us separate sand from water; floating materials are used for boats, rafts and life jackets.
topics.example: When making nimbu pani, sugar and salt dissolve in the water (soluble), lemon juice mixes in, but a few lemon seeds that fall in sink to the bottom and don't dissolve.
keyPoints: Soluble: dissolves in water (salt, sugar)
Insoluble: does not dissolve (sand, chalk, sawdust)
ORS = salt + sugar dissolved in clean water
Some liquids mix with water (lemon juice), some don't (oil)
Oxygen dissolves in water and helps aquatic animals breathe
Float: wood, cork, oil; sink: stone, iron nail, coin

topics.title: Transparent, translucent and opaque
topics.summary: Transparent materials let us see clearly through them (clear glass, water); translucent materials let us see only partly (butter paper, frosted glass); opaque materials don't let us see through at all (wood, metal, cardboard).
topics.simple: You can see clearly through **transparent** things like window glass and clean water. You can see only a little, blurred, through **translucent** things like butter paper or frosted glass. You can't see through **opaque** things at all, like a wooden door or a steel plate.
topics.explain:
Materials can be grouped by **how much we can see through them**.

- **Transparent:** we can see **clearly** through them
  - Examples: clear glass, clean water, air, some clear plastics, cellophane
  - Used in windows, spectacles, car windscreens, showcases

- **Translucent:** we can see through them **only partly** (not clearly)
  - Examples: butter paper, frosted glass, oiled paper, thin tissue paper, a thin plastic bag
  - Used in bathroom windows and lamp shades, where light is wanted but privacy is also needed

- **Opaque:** we **cannot see through them at all**
  - Examples: wood, metal, cardboard, stone, a brick wall, thick cloth
  - Used for doors, walls and boxes

**Simple test:** look at a lit torch or bulb through the material. If you see the light clearly, it's transparent; dimly or blurred, translucent; not at all, opaque.

A piece of paper is opaque, but if you put a drop of oil on it, that spot becomes translucent.
topics.example: In many homes, the living room window has clear glass (transparent) to see outside, the bathroom window has frosted glass (translucent) for privacy, and the main door is made of wood (opaque).
keyPoints: Transparent: see clearly through (clear glass, water, air)
Translucent: see partly through (butter paper, frosted glass)
Opaque: cannot see through (wood, metal, cardboard)
Test by looking at a lit torch through the material
Oiled paper changes from opaque to translucent

topics.title: Grouping materials and what is matter
topics.summary: Grouping materials by their properties makes them easier to study and use. Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space; mass is measured in kilograms and grams, and the space taken (volume) in litres and millilitres.
topics.simple: We can sort materials into groups — shiny or dull, hard or soft, soluble or insoluble, transparent or opaque. This helps us find and use them. Everything that has **mass** (weight) and takes up **space** is called **matter**: water, air, wood, your own body. Light and sound are not matter.
topics.explain:
**Grouping materials**
We group materials by a property we choose: lustrous/non-lustrous, hard/soft, soluble/insoluble, floats/sinks, transparent/translucent/opaque. The **same material** can fall into different groups for different properties. For example, glass is hard, transparent, insoluble and sinks. Grouping makes it easier to:
- Study and compare materials
- Store things in an organised way (like a kitchen or a shop)
- Choose the right material for a job

**Mass: how heavy or light?**
If you fill three identical cups with water, sand and pebbles, they feel different in weight. The amount of matter in an object is its **mass**.
- Units: **kilogram (kg)** and **gram (g)**
- **1 kg = 1000 g**

**Volume: space taken up**
Every object takes up space. The amount of space is its **volume**.
- Liquid volume units: **litre (L)** and **millilitre (mL)**
- **1 L = 1000 mL**
- The same amount of water looks different in a tall narrow glass and a wide bowl, but its volume is the same.

**What is matter?** **Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space.**
- Matter: water, air, wood, sand, milk, our bodies (air has mass and fills balloons and tyres)
- Not matter: light, sound, heat, feelings, thoughts — they don't have mass or take up space
topics.example: A blown-up balloon or a pumped-up bicycle tyre shows that air takes up space, and a full gas cylinder weighs more than an empty one — so gases are matter too.
keyPoints: Group materials by a chosen property
One material can belong to several groups
Mass = amount of matter; 1 kg = 1000 g
Volume = space occupied; 1 L = 1000 mL
Matter = anything that has mass and occupies space
Air is matter; light, sound and feelings are not

keyConcepts.meaning: A thing with a definite shape and use, such as a chair or a bottle.
The substance an object is made of, such as wood, metal, plastic or glass.
Having a shiny surface, like most metals.
Dull in appearance, like wood, paper or clay.
Hard materials are difficult to scratch or compress; soft ones are easy to scratch or compress.
Able to dissolve in water, like salt and sugar.
Does not dissolve in water, like sand and chalk.
Lets us see clearly through it, like clear glass.
Lets us see through it only partly, like butter paper or frosted glass.
Does not let us see through it at all, like wood or metal.
Anything that has mass and occupies space.
Mass is the amount of matter (kg, g); volume is the space taken up (L, mL).

commonMistakes: Confusing an object with its material — a spoon is an object; steel is the material.
Thinking all materials that look dull are non-metals — metals can go dull in air but shine when freshly cut or polished.
Mixing up translucent and transparent — translucent lets you see only partly.
Thinking air is not matter because we can't see it — it has mass and occupies space.
Calling light, sound or heat matter — they have no mass and take up no space.
Thinking a material belongs to only one group — glass is hard, transparent and insoluble at the same time.
revision: Objects are made of materials; one object can be made of different materials.
Materials are chosen based on the use of the object.
Hard: difficult to scratch/compress; soft: easy to scratch/compress.
Soluble: salt, sugar. Insoluble: sand, chalk, sawdust.
ORS = salt + sugar dissolved in clean water.
Oil doesn't mix with water; lemon juice and vinegar do.
Float: wood, cork, oil. Sink: stone, iron nail.
Matter = anything with mass that occupies space.
Air is matter; light, sound and feelings are not.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an object and a material?
faqs.a: An **object** is a thing with a shape and use, like a chair. A **material** is what it is made of, like wood or plastic. A chair (object) can be made of wood, plastic or metal (materials).

faqs.q: What is the difference between transparent, translucent and opaque?
faqs.a:
- **Transparent:** see clearly through it (clear glass, water)
- **Translucent:** see partly, blurred (butter paper, frosted glass)
- **Opaque:** can't see through at all (wood, metal, cardboard)
Yes. Air has mass and takes up space. A balloon or tyre becomes bigger when air is filled in, showing air takes up space, and a filled gas cylinder is heavier than an empty one.

faqs.q: Why are cooking pans made of metal but their handles of plastic or wood?
faqs.a: Metal can take high heat and passes heat to the food quickly, which is good for cooking. Plastic and wood don't get hot quickly, so a handle made of them is safe to hold.

quiz.q: In the object 'steel spoon', steel is the:
quiz.explain: The spoon is the object; steel is the material it's made of.
Metals like copper are shiny (lustrous); the others are dull.

quiz.q: Which of these is the softest?
quiz.explain: Cotton is easily compressed; the others are hard.

quiz.q: Which substance is insoluble in water?
quiz.explain: Sand does not dissolve however long you stir it.

quiz.q: ORS is prepared by dissolving which substances in clean water?
quiz.explain: ORS is salt and sugar dissolved in clean water.

quiz.q: Which liquid does NOT mix with water and forms a separate layer?
quiz.explain: Oils don't mix with water; they float as a separate layer.

quiz.q: Frosted glass used in bathroom windows is:
quiz.explain: Frosted glass lets light through but you can't see clearly through it.
You can't see through wood at all.

options: Can be seen with the eyes
quiz.explain: Matter has mass and takes up space — even invisible air.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT matter?
quiz.explain: Light has no mass and doesn't occupy space, so it is not matter.

quiz.q: How many millilitres are there in 2.5 litres?
Why is a cooking pan usually given a plastic or wooden handle?
options: Plastic and wood dissolve in water
Plastic and wood do not get hot quickly, so the handle is safe to hold
quiz.explain: Materials are chosen for their job; plastic and wood don't heat up quickly like metal.
